Geog 4/6300: Lab 3-Confidence intervals

Confidence intervals

Your name: Mary Elizabeth Rudd

Overview:

In this lab, we will create confidence intervals for January precipitation in Washington during two time periods: 1950-1969 and 2005-2024. Using county-level precipitation data from the ERA5 dataset, you will estimate statewide precipitation patterns, then examine variation and change at the county level. We’ve summed the precipitation in January for each county over two twenty year time periods: 1950-1969 and 2005-2024. You’ll be using those data to create confidence intervals at a state and county level.

To load these data, load the csv file, which is included in the data folder:

era5_data<-read_csv("~/Downloads/Local GEOG Notes:Projects/geog4300_lab3/data/precip_uswest_era5.csv")

This is a long format dataset including county identifiers, county population, median household income, and poverty rate. Census figures are based on the 2018-22 ACS. The last two columns (year, prcp_m, time_range) give the year and total precipitation in meters from the ERA5 NetCDF file, and two time ranges (1950-1969 and 2005-2024).

The script used to create this dataframe is also provided in this repository (‘lab3_dataprep’), along with rasters of the yearly mean total precipitation for Januaries in the two time periods of interest.

For this lab to be marked complete, it must demonstrate the following learning standards:

    1. Create effective data visualizations across multiple chart types (line, scatter, histogram, Q-Q plot), applying appropriate aesthetic choices such as color, grouping, and labeling. (Tasks 2 and 5)
    1. Produce and interpret confidence interval plots that enable visual comparison of means and uncertainty across groups or time periods. (Tasks 2, 3, 5, and 6)
    1. Visualize spatial data using appropriate mapping tools, selecting suitable classification schemes and cartographic elements to support clear communication. (Task 7)
    1. Arrange and present tabular results in a readable format appropriate for a technical document or report. (Tasks 1 and 4)
    1. Use measures of central tendency and dispersion to describe the variables in tabular datasets (Tasks 1 and 4)
    1. Explaining how evidence from a sample supports conclusions about a population while acknowledging sampling variability and uncertainty. (Tasks 3 and 6)
    1. Construct and interpret confidence intervals, explaining how factors such as sample size and spatial scale affect the precision of an estimate. (Tasks 1, 3, 4 and 6)

Part 1: Calculating statewide confidence intervals for Washington’s precipitation

In the first part of this lab, you’ll determine a confidence interval for Washington’s precipitation for these two time periods. This can be helpful in identifying whether precipitation has changed across the state (e.g., whether the two confidence intervals overlap) using the county data as your sample.

Task 1 Load the data and filter it to just include data for the state of Washington. Then create a table showing mean precipitation, standard deviation, number of observations (sample size), and upper/lower confidence interval bounds for each of the two time periods in the time_range field. Use kable to display the table when you are done.

era5_WA<-era5_data %>%
  filter(st_name=="Washington") %>% #Filters for state of WA
  group_by(time_range) %>%
  summarise(
    mean_prcp=mean(prcp_m, na.rm = TRUE),
    sd_prcp=sd(prcp_m, na.rm = TRUE),
    observation_count=sum(!is.na(prcp_m)),
    se=sd_prcp / sqrt(observation_count),
    lower_ci=mean_prcp - qt(0.975, df = observation_count - 1) * se,
    upper_ci=mean_prcp + qt(0.975, df = observation_count - 1) * se)

era5_WA%>%
  kable()
time_range mean_prcp sd_prcp observation_count se lower_ci upper_ci
1950-69 0.2032239 0.1562948 780 0.0055963 0.1922383 0.2142094
2005-24 0.1664626 0.1230138 780 0.0044046 0.1578163 0.1751089

Using the code provided in class, create a ggplot graphic that visualizes these two confidence intervals. You’ll want to use geom_point and geom_linerange to do so. Use states as the y-axis and mean precipitation as the x axis. Vary the color and position of the dots and lines for the mean/CI by the time_range variable. Feel free to also experiment with axis labels/themes to make the graph more appealing and accessible.

Task 2 Create a ggplot graphic as described above to show the confidence intervals for precipitation in Washington for each time range.

ggplot(era5_WA) +
  geom_linerange(aes(xmin = lower_ci, xmax = upper_ci, y = time_range, color = time_range)) +
  geom_point(aes(x = mean_prcp, y = time_range, color = time_range)) +
  scale_color_manual(values = c("#4e6d58", "#836685")) +  
  labs(x = "Mean January Precipitation (m)", y = "Time period", color = "Time period") +
  theme_minimal()

Task 3 Interpret your table and graph. What do they tell us about the change in Washington’s precipitation during this time?

In Washington, the mean level of precipitation in 1950-1969 was 0.203 meters, and 0.166 meters in 2005-2024. This shows a change of about 0.037 meters of rainfall. The 95% confidence interval for 1950-1969 runs from 0.1922383 to 0.2142094, and for 2005-2024 the CI ran from 0.1578163 to 0.1751089. The intervals do not overlap, there seems to be some evidence that the statewide mean changed between the time periods of 1950-1969 and 2005-2024.

Part 2: Analyzing county data in Washington.

In part 1, you ran a state level analysis. What if you wanted to identify where populations might be negatively affected by precipitation changes within a state? In this section, you’ll look at the changes in precipitation at county level in Washington to

To start with, adapt your code from step 1 so that you create confidence intervals for counties instead of states. After creating that dataset, create another ggplot graph of those confidence intervals that you can compare to the state level data in Task 2 to examine how precipitation has changed across counties in Washington.

Task 4 Create a summary table for January precipitation in Washington counties for both time periods. Use the same approach as in Task 1, but calculate statistics for counties rather than the state as a whole. Call the head of your table with kable when you are done.

era5_WA_CTY<-era5_data %>%
   filter(st_name =="Washington",month(year) == 1) %>%
  group_by(cty_name,time_range) %>%
  summarise(
    mean_prcp=mean(prcp_m, na.rm = TRUE),
    sd_prcp=sd(prcp_m, na.rm = TRUE),
    observation_count=sum(!is.na(prcp_m)),
    se=sd_prcp / sqrt(observation_count),
    lower_ci=mean_prcp - qt(0.975, df = observation_count - 1) * se,
    upper_ci=mean_prcp + qt(0.975, df = observation_count - 1) * se)

Task 5 Visualize the confidence intervals for the county-level data you generated in task 4, using the same style as you did for Task 2 above. For an optional extra challenge, visually highlight the counties where the confidence intervals between time periods do NOT overlap.

cty_overlap <- era5_WA_CTY %>%
  group_by(cty_name) %>%
  summarise(no_overlap = max(lower_ci) > min(upper_ci))  

era5_WA_CTY_plot <- era5_WA_CTY %>%
  left_join(cty_overlap, by = "cty_name")

ggplot(era5_WA_CTY_plot,
       aes(y = reorder(cty_name, mean_prcp), color = time_range)) +
  geom_linerange(aes(xmin = lower_ci, xmax = upper_ci, linewidth = no_overlap), position = position_dodge(width = 0.6)) +
  geom_point(aes(x = mean_prcp, size = no_overlap), position = position_dodge(width = 0.6)) +
  scale_color_manual(values = c("#4e6d58", "#836685")) +        
  scale_linewidth_manual(values = c(`TRUE` = 2, `FALSE` = 0.5), guide = "none") +
  scale_size_manual(values = c(`TRUE` = 4, `FALSE` = 1.5), guide = "none") +
  labs(x = "Mean January Precipitation (m)", y = "County", color = "Time period")+
  theme_minimal()

Task 6: Compare the size of the error terms for your county level data to the error terms at state level that you calculated in Task 1. Are they bigger or smaller? Explain why the formula you used for calculating the error terms produced error terms of different sizes. How is this difference visible in your ggplot graphs?

THe standard error of the data on a state level is around 0.004 - 0.005 meters, while the county data varies much more from county to county. Some of the standard errors at the county level are as large as 0.04m, and as small as 0.003m. When we look at the standard error on the state level vs county level, the n term we use in calculating standard error (SE = s / √n) is very large when we are grouping all the data by just time range. The n is much smaller when we isolate just the january occurrences and further group things by county. BEcause the n is smaller, the standard error for the county level is larger at the county level. This is consistent with our visualization, as we see the county standard errors overlapping more than the state.

Task 7: Transform the county data from task 4 into wide format so that the means for each time period are in the same row for each county. Then calculate the change in precipitation between the time periods. Join this table to the geopackage file that contains county boundaries and census data, making sure that you only have Washington counties included - use the geopackage data/acsdata_cty_westreg.gpkg. Then use tmap to map out the difference in precipitation means across the two time periods. Make sure the legend of this map is interpretable.

era5_CTY_Wide <- era5_WA_CTY %>%
  ungroup() %>%
  select(cty_name, time_range, mean_prcp) %>%
  pivot_wider(names_from = time_range, values_from = mean_prcp) %>%
  rename(`1950-1969` = 2, `2005-2024` = 3) %>%
  mutate(prcp_change = `2005-2024` - `1950-1969`)

  head() %>%
  kable(digits = 4)

Optional challenge section: Interpreting the implications of precipitation changes

Now that you’ve calculated these means and confidence intervals, let’s identify who might be most affected by changes in precipitation. To see who is affected, create a dummy variable that flags any counties with a decline of 5 centimeters or more (0.05 meters) with a 1, labeling all other counties with a 0. Use group_by and summarise to do the following:

  • Count the total population in each of these two county groups.
  • Calculate the mean value for median income and poverty rate in these two groups.

Task 8 Create a dummy variable for counties with a change of 0.05 meters or more between the time periods. Calculate how many people currently live in these counties along with the mean value of median income (medinc) and poverty rate (pov_pop_pct) for those areas.

wa_challenge <- wa_cty_data %>%                                 
  mutate(decline = if_else(prcp_change <= -0.05, 1, 0))   # 1 = dropped 0.05 m or more

wa_challenge %>%
  group_by(decline) %>%
  summarise(
    n_counties  = n(),
    total_pop   = sum(totpop_race, na.rm = TRUE),
    mean_medinc = mean(medinc, na.rm = TRUE),
    mean_pov    = mean(pov_pop_pct, na.rm = TRUE)
  ) %>%
  kable()

Task 9 Create a one paragraph summary of your results from tasks 7 and 8. What do you learn about how precipitation has changed in the last 70 years across the state of Washington? How would you describe the population affected by large drops in precipitation based on your results?

Between 1950-1969 and 2005-2024, mean January precipitation in Washington decreased by about 0.037 m statewide, and the 95% confidence intervals for the two periods did not overlap. At the county level, county confidence intervals overlap more often and varies alot from county to county. 15 of 39 counties in Washington saw precipitation declines by 0.05 meters or more, and about 3.37 million people live in those counties total. Compared with the other counties that did not see those declines, the counties with the 0.05+ declines have a higher mean median household income and a lower mean poverty rate. The population affected by large drops in precipitation seems to be slightly better off economically than the rest of the state.

Small multiples or multi-panel maps are often a helpful way to show change over time. See this page for more information about how these are created in tmap:

  • https://r-tmap.github.io/tmap/articles/basics_facets

Using these tools, create a small multiples map of your precipitation data for counties in a state of your choice for all 40 years in these two time periods. This means you will have one figure with 40 individual maps, all of the same state in different years. These maps should allow easy comparison across years and should be clearly labeled so that they could be interpreted by someone with no knowledge of this assignment.

In addition, describe two interesting trends you see in the figure you created.

wa_yearly <- wa_cty_data %>%
  select(cty_name) %>%
  inner_join(
    era5_data %>%
      filter(st_name == "Washington") %>%
      mutate(yr = factor(year(year))) %>%
      select(cty_name, yr, prcp_m),
    by = "cty_name")

tm_shape(wa_yearly) +
  tm_polygons("prcp_m",
              lwd = 0.2,
              fill.legend = tm_legend(title = "January\nprecipitation (m)", title.size = 0.7, text.size = 0.6)) +
  tm_facets_wrap("yr", nrow = 5, ncol = 8) +
  tm_layout(scale = 0.3, inner.margins = 0, outer.margins = 0, between_margin = 0, panel.label.size = 0.7)

Two patterns: First, the level of january precipitation is pretty consistent from west to east, with eastern Washington seeing significantly less precipitation. This is consistent from what I know about how mountains impact rainfall. The part of the state east of the Cascades gets significantly less rainfall, as the air passes over the mountain peaks and warms, causing rain clouds to dissipate. The second thing I noticed is that that there are some years (1953 and 2020) that seem to be pretty extreme with rainfall. There also seems to be more rainfall in the 1950-1969 maps compared to the more recent maps.
